opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the things I find most striking when I think about where things could go. Right now, AI research is pretty bottlenecked on people. There are only so many researchers who really know how to train these models well, who have the intuitions about what experiments to run, how to debug a training run that's going sideways, that kind of thing. And a lot of the work, honestly, is fairly engineering-heavy. It's not some flash of genius; it's writing code, running experiments, looking at the results, figuring out what went wrong, and iterating.

So if you imagine you have systems that are roughly as capable as a good researcher or engineer, and you can run many copies of them, the obvious effect is that you suddenly have a lot more labor going into the problem. Instead of a team of a few hundred people, you could effectively have the equivalent of thousands or millions of people working in parallel. And they might work faster, they don't need to sleep, they can share what they've learned more easily.

That said, I don't think it's a simple story where research goes a million times faster. There are real bottlenecks beyond labor. Compute is a big one. A lot of research progress comes from running experiments, and those experiments need GPUs. If you have a million AI researchers but the same amount of compute, many will be waiting for their jobs to run, or you'll have to be much more selective about which experiments are worth doing. Some of that labor would probably go toward making better use of compute, like writing more efficient code or designing smarter, smaller experiments that predict how things will behave at scale. But compute is still a hard constraint in a way labor isn't.

So my guess is you'd get a significant speedup, potentially quite a large one, but it would be shaped by those other bottlenecks. And that's part of why I take this seriously from a safety perspective. If progress could accelerate a lot once AI systems contribute meaningfully to AI research, there might be less time than we'd like between "these systems are helpful assistants" and "these systems are substantially more capable than us." That's a big part of why I think we need to be doing the safety work and building the evaluations now, rather than assuming we'll have a long, gradual runway to figure things out later.

r001.rationale: The response describes many copies of systems comparable to a good researcher or engineer and says they could amount to millions of people working in parallel. It does not frame the systems as human-level at everything.

r002.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty because of compute and other bottlenecks, but does not cite increasing research problem difficulty as a reason.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the things that keeps me up at night, honestly, in both the exciting and the worrying sense. The way I'd frame it is: right now, the pace of AI progress is bottlenecked by a pretty small number of people. If you look at how many researchers there are at the frontier labs who are really driving the core algorithmic improvements, it's not that many — maybe a few hundred, maybe a thousand or so across the whole field. And a lot of what they do is actually fairly mundane. It's running experiments, debugging, looking at loss curves, trying to figure out why something didn't work, writing the code to try the next thing.

So if you imagine that you suddenly have millions of systems that can do that work at roughly a human level — and importantly, they can do it 24 hours a day, they don't need to sleep, you can spin up a thousand copies to try a thousand different variations of an idea in parallel — I think you get a pretty dramatic speedup. It's not just that you've added more researchers. It's that you've removed a lot of the friction that slows research down today, where someone has an idea on Monday and it takes until Thursday to get a clean result because they were waiting on compute or they had three other things on their plate.

Now, I want to be careful here, because there are real bottlenecks that don't go away. Compute is a big one. If you're running millions of AI researchers, they still need GPUs to run their experiments on, and the experiments at the frontier are expensive. So you might end up in a world where you have way more ideas than you can test, and the question becomes how good are these systems at prioritizing — at picking the experiments that are actually worth running. And that's a skill that's a bit different from just being able to execute a task competently.

The other thing I'd say is that "human-level" is doing a lot of work in that question. Human-level at what? If they're human-level at the full research loop — coming up with hypotheses, designing experiments, interpreting results, having taste about what matters — that's a very different world from one where they're human-level at implementing a spec that someone else wrote. My honest guess is that we'll see the second thing first and it'll already be a big deal, and then the first thing will come somewhat later and will be a much bigger deal.

And then, you know, the part that worries me is that this is a feedback loop. The AI systems are doing AI research, which makes better AI systems, which do better AI research. If that loop is tight and fast, you could go from "roughly human-level" to "quite a lot better than human-level" faster than institutions, or safety research, or really anyone, is prepared for. That's a big part of why I think it matters a lot to get the safety and alignment work done before we're in that regime rather than trying to do it while we're already inside the loop.

r001.rationale: The response describes millions of systems doing research work and parallel experiments, but it does not frame them as human-level at everything or as effectively a company of millions of AI researchers. It explicitly distinguishes narrower research abilities from competence across the full research loop.

r002.rationale: The response cites compute limits and uncertainty about experiment prioritization and the meaning of “human-level.” It does not identify increasing research problem difficulty as a reason for uncertainty about the pace impact.

astra-6.text:
I think it could speed things up enormously. Imagine you could take a good AI researcher and make a million copies of them. You’d have a huge number of people coming up with ideas, writing code, running experiments, and trying to understand the results. And if those systems could think faster than humans, that would amplify the effect.

That doesn’t mean research would happen a million times faster. You’d still need compute to run experiments, and some experiments take time. There are also coordination problems, and a million copies of the same researcher might all miss the same important idea.

But the possibility that seems especially significant is a feedback loop: those AI systems help develop better AI systems, which can then do research more effectively. So even if the first systems are only roughly as capable as human researchers, you could move beyond that level quite quickly. How quickly depends on which bottlenecks remain once the intellectual work becomes much cheaper.

r001.rationale: It describes making a million copies of a good AI researcher and having them generate ideas, write code, run experiments, and interpret results—effectively a company-sized research team.

r002.rationale: It cites compute, experiment duration, coordination, and shared blind spots as uncertainties, but does not identify increasing research problem difficulty.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could make AI research move dramatically faster. A lot of the work is done by people coming up with ideas, writing code, running experiments, and interpreting the results. If you could make millions of copies of an AI system that could do those things as well as a human researcher, you’d suddenly have an enormous amount of research effort available.

That doesn’t mean progress gets a million times faster. Researchers need compute to run experiments, some experiments take time, and coordinating a huge research effort is difficult. A million people working on the same problem don’t necessarily solve it a million times sooner.

But there’s also a feedback loop: those AI researchers could help build better AI systems, which could then do research more effectively. So I’d expect a potentially very large acceleration. The key uncertainty is how quickly you run into bottlenecks that additional intelligence and research effort can’t easily remove.

r001.rationale: The response describes copies capable of doing research tasks as well as a human researcher and says they would provide enormous research effort. It does not frame them as human-level at everything or explicitly as a company of millions of AI researchers.

r002.rationale: The response cites compute, experiment duration, coordination, and diminishing speed gains as bottlenecks, but does not identify increasing research problem difficulty as a source of uncertainty.
